REQUEST
explain how the learning rate affects gradient descent — show a ball rolling down a loss curve with a good rate, then one that is too large and overshoots, then one that is too small and never arrives

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [14s] Draw the loss curve and mark its true minimum -- Here is a loss curve. Every point along it is one setting of our parameter, and the height is how badly the model does there. Somewhere down in that valley is the best setting.
2. [10s] Place a ball on the slope and show the gradient -- Start anywhere. The slope under your feet tells you which way is downhill — and how steep it is tells you how far to step.
3. [10s] A good learning rate walks the ball to the minimum -- Step a fraction of that slope, again and again. That fraction is the learning rate. Get it right and you walk straight into the valley.
4. [12s] Too large a step and it climbs out of the valley -- But make that fraction too big and each step overshoots the bottom, landing further up the other side. The steps grow, and you climb out of the valley entirely.
5. [10s] Too small and it never arrives -- Too small, and every step is timid. You are heading the right way, but you will run out of patience long before you arrive.
6. [12s] The three rates side by side -- Too small crawls. Too large diverges. The whole art is finding the step that is just big enough to make progress, and just small enough to stay in the valley.
END

1. [24s] Footage of IMO competition hall. -- In 2025, over 600 teenagers from all around the world gathered in the Sunshine Coast of Australia to compete in the International Math Olympiad. This contest consists of six highly challenging problems, and problem number six was the hardest by far. Despite every participant there clearly being a world class problem solver among the best of their country, less than 1% of the students managed to get full marks on it.
2. [22s] Animated text: "IMO Problem 6". -- It also seems likely to be the last IMO problem to be solved. No problem that AI could not solve. And that sentence would have sounded ridiculous to most people familiar with contest math even as few as five years ago, I think it's fair to say. If you're outside this world, the thing you have to understand is that these problems are designed to require elements of imagination and creativity. It's not at all just rote memorization or computation.
3. [31s] Scrolling LaTeX proof on screen. -- To solve one of these problems does not simply mean giving a correct numerical answer or anything like that. It means writing up a full rigorous proof, and the spirit of the contest is that the act of finding a proof should require gaining a nuanced and deep understanding of some particular setup. So if we step back in time, say to 2021, even though by then there had been plenty of impressive results with AI in games, and even though by then scaling laws for natural language had become clear, a lot of people would have seen the IMO as a different ballgame entirely.
4. [29s] Timeline graphic showing 2023-2024 progress. -- It requires this mixture of rigor and creativity, and the search space of logical moves that you can make when you're writing up a proof is effectively infinite. In fact, when I was on Dwarkesh Patel's podcast in 2023, this was one of his questions. By the time that an AI model can get gold in the International Math Olympiad, is that just AGI? But just the very next year, in 2024, Google DeepMind's AlphaProof team produced a model that answered four out of the six questions on that year's exam.
5. [29s] Lean code snippet next to text. -- There is a slight asterisk here because that system required that humans manually translate the problems from English into Lean, which is basically a programming language where mathematical proofs are programs. But the AlphaProof system was handling the substance of finding the proof, even if it was just in a different language, and that alone was a surprise to many. And then in 2025 multiple different organizations had their models try the test, and this time there was a mixture of those taking the Lean approach and some doing it purely with natural language end to end.
6. [28s] Checkmarks appearing next to six problems. -- And now models answered every single question on the contest, except for this problem number six. And then by 2026... Simply prompting reasoning models that are available to the public would be enough to get correct answers on all six problems. And that really undersells exactly how far these models have come over the last few years when it comes to doing math. The IMO almost feels like ancient history as a benchmark, as everything has speed run its way into the domain of research math over the last year.

It's named after its inventors Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman, and it's based on the mathematical properties of prime numbers and modular arithmetic. The RSA algorithm is based on the idea that it's easy to multiply two large prime numbers together, but it's extremely difficult to factor the product back into its original primes. This asymmetry is what makes RSA secure.

3. [19s] Euler's totient function, φ(n). -- Next, we need to calculate Euler's totient function, φ(n), which counts the number of integers up to n that are relatively prime to n. For n equals p times q, φ(n) equals (p minus 1) times (q minus 1). So, φ(3233) equals (61 minus 1) times (53 minus 1), which equals 60 times 52, or 3120.
4. [20s] Public exponent, e. -- Now, we need to choose a public exponent, e, which is a number that's relatively prime to φ(n). The public exponent, e, is part of the public key, which is used to encrypt messages.
5. [18s] Private exponent, d. -- The private exponent, d, is calculated using the modular multiplicative inverse of e modulo φ(n). In other words, d is the number that satisfies the equation e times d equals 1 modulo φ(n). For our example, d equals 2753. 3. [12s] Write the action integral -- The action integral is given by the integral from time t1 to t2 of the Lagrangian L(q(t), q'(t), t) dt, where q(t) is the generalized coordinate of the system, and q'(t) is its time derivative.
4. [14s] Explain the variational problem -- The principle of least action is a variational problem, where we seek the path q(t) that minimizes the action integral. This is done by considering small variations around the actual path and requiring that the first variation of the action integral vanishes.
5. [9s] Derive Euler-Lagrange equations -- The condition that the first variation of the action integral vanishes leads to the Euler-Lagrange equations, which are second-order ordinary differential equations for the generalized coordinates q(t).
6. [8s] Show the equivalence to Newton's laws -- The Euler-Lagrange equations can be shown to be equivalent to Newton's laws of motion, demonstrating the consistency of Lagrangian mechanics with classical mechanics.

1. [38s] A sequence of numbers on a number line. -- Alright, folks, let's dive into the foundation of real analysis. Today, we're going to talk about something called Cauchy sequences. Now, you might be thinking, "What's a Cauchy sequence?" Well, imagine you're walking along a number line, and you're dropping little pebbles at each step. These pebbles represent a sequence of numbers. The interesting thing about Cauchy sequences is that as you walk further down the line, the pebbles get closer and closer to each other. But here's the twist: you don't necessarily know where they're heading, or if they're heading anywhere at all. It's like you're in a fog, and you can only see the pebbles getting closer, but you can't see the endpoint.
2. [30s] Pebbles getting closer together on a number line. -- So, let's say you drop your first pebble at 0. Then, you take a step and drop another pebble at 0.1. Then, you take another step and drop a third pebble at 0.11. And so on. You can see that the pebbles are getting closer together, but you don't know if they're getting closer to a specific number, or if they're just getting closer to each other. That's what makes Cauchy sequences special. They're sequences where the terms get arbitrarily close to each other, but you don't necessarily know their limit.
3. [25s] Definition of a Cauchy sequence. -- Now, let's formalize this. A sequence (aₙ) is called a Cauchy sequence if for every ε greater than 0, there exists an N such that for all n, m greater than or equal to N, the distance between aₙ and aₘ is less than ε. In simpler terms, no matter how small a distance you pick, you can find a point in the sequence after which all the terms are within that distance of each other.
4. [22s] Visualizing the definition with pebbles. -- So, going back to our pebbles, for any distance you pick, say 0.01, you can find a point after which all the pebbles are within 0.01 of each other. Then, if you pick a smaller distance, say 0.001, you can find another point after which all the pebbles are within 0.001 of each other. And so on. This is the essence of a Cauchy sequence.
5. [23s] A sequence converging to a limit. -- Now, you might be thinking, "But if the sequence is Cauchy, does it necessarily converge to a limit?" Well, in the real number system, the answer is yes. This is known as Cauchy's convergence criterion. If a sequence is Cauchy, then it converges to a limit. And this is what makes the real number system complete. There are no missing gaps or holes for a converging sequence to fall through.
6. [22s] A sequence that's Cauchy but not convergent. -- But here's the thing: not all number systems are complete. For example, in the rational number system, there are Cauchy sequences that don't converge to a limit. A classic example is the sequence of decimal approximations of √2. 1. [11s] Draw a surface and its boundary edge -- Imagine a surface, like a sheet of paper, and its boundary edge, like the border around it. The surface is a two-dimensional object, and the edge is a one-dimensional curve that goes around it.
2. [15s] Introduce a vector field on the surface -- Now, imagine tiny arrows, called vectors, sticking out from every point on the surface. These vectors form a vector field, and they can point in any direction, up, down, or sideways. The direction and length of each vector can change from point to point.
3. [17s] Define the flux of the vector field through the surface -- The flux is a measure of how much of the vector field is going through the surface. It's like counting how many vectors are pointing in or out of the surface. If most vectors are pointing out, the flux is positive. If most are pointing in, the flux is negative.
4. [17s] Introduce a line integral around the boundary edge -- Now, let's look at the boundary edge. We can calculate a line integral around this edge. It's like adding up the dot product of the vector field with the tiny segments of the edge. The dot product tells us how much of each vector is pointing in the direction of the edge.
5. [17s] State Stokes' theorem -- Stokes' theorem says that the flux of the vector field through the surface is equal to the line integral around the boundary edge. In other words, the total amount of the vector field going through the surface is the same as the sum of the vector field along the edge.
6. [20s] Explain the physical meaning of Stokes' theorem -- Think of the vector field as representing a fluid flow. The flux through the surface is the net flow of the fluid through the surface, and the line integral around the edge is the circulation of the fluid around the edge. Stokes' theorem tells us that the net flow through the surface is equal to the circulation around the edge.

1. [21s] Animated 3D sphere with a hole. -- In this video, we're going to explore a powerful tool in algebraic topology called the Mayer-Vietoris sequence. It's a way to break down the computation of homology groups, which are a way to study the "shape" of spaces. To start, let's consider a simple example: a sphere with a hole. This is a 2-dimensional space, and we want to understand its homology groups.
2. [20s] Two overlapping 3D spheres. -- The Mayer-Vietoris sequence is based on the idea of covering a space with two open sets that overlap. In this case, we can cover our sphere with a hole with two open sets: one that's a larger sphere, and one that's a smaller sphere. The intersection of these two open sets is an annulus, which is a ring-shaped space.
3. [21s] Diagram of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence. -- The Mayer-Vietoris sequence is a long exact sequence that relates the homology groups of the two open sets, the homology group of their intersection, and the homology group of the original space. It's a bit abstract, but we can start to see how it works by looking at the diagram. The sequence starts with the homology group of the intersection, which is the annulus.
4. [22s] Animated annulus. -- The annulus is a 2-dimensional space, so its first homology group is the infinite cyclic group, which we can think of as the integers. The second homology group is zero, because the annulus is contractible. The Mayer-Vietoris sequence tells us that the first homology group of the sphere with a hole is the same as the first homology group of the intersection, which is the integers.
5. [22s] Animated sphere with a hole. -- But what about the second homology group? The Mayer-Vietoris sequence tells us that it's the same as the second homology group of the union of the two open sets, which is the sphere with a hole. The sphere with a hole is a 2-dimensional space, so its second homology group is the integers. This makes sense, because the sphere with a hole has a non-trivial 2-dimensional hole.
6. [21s] Diagram of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence with labels. -- Now, let's look at the Mayer-Vietoris sequence in more detail. The sequence starts with the homology group of the intersection, which is the annulus. The next term is the direct sum of the homology groups of the two open sets, which are both the integers. The next term is the homology group of the sphere with a hole, which is the integers.

1. [30s] Text title, Lagrange multipliers animation. -- So, in my video about optimization problems, we discussed how to find the maximum or minimum of a function subject to a constraint. We used the method of Lagrange multipliers, but it was a little bit too much detail, so I ended up cutting it out of the video. So what I wanted to do here is just show you a condensed version of that, because it references a pretty clever argument by Mark Levi, and it also gives a sense of completion to the optimization problem as a whole.
2. [17s] Contour plot of a function. -- Consider a function f(x, y) that we want to optimize. We can represent this function using a contour plot, where each contour line represents a constant value of the function. The goal is to find the points on the contour plot that correspond to the maximum or minimum of the function.
3. [14s] Constraint curve on the contour plot. -- Now, let's say we have a constraint g(x, y) = c, which we can represent as a curve on the contour plot. We want to find the points on this curve that correspond to the maximum or minimum of the function f(x, y).
4. [15s] Tangent line to the constraint curve. -- The key idea behind Lagrange multipliers is to find the points where the contour lines of f(x, y) are tangent to the constraint curve g(x, y) = c. At these points, the gradient of f(x, y) is parallel to the gradient of g(x, y).
5. [14s] Lagrange multiplier equation. -- To find these points, we can set up the Lagrange multiplier equation: ∇f(x, y) = λ∇g(x, y). This equation tells us that the gradient of f(x, y) is a scalar multiple of the gradient of g(x, y), where λ is the Lagrange multiplier.
6. [20s] Solving the system of equations. -- To solve for x, y, and λ, we need to set up a system of equations consisting of the constraint equation g(x, y) = c and the Lagrange multiplier equation ∇f(x, y) = λ∇g(x, y). We can then solve this system of equations to find the critical points of the function f(x, y) subject to the constraint g(x, y) = c.

1. [21s] Text title, factorial function, discrete points. -- So, you know how sometimes we need to calculate large factorials, like 100 factorial? It's a huge number, and calculating it directly can be computationally intensive. That's where the Stirling approximation comes in. It's a way to estimate factorials using continuous curves, which can be much easier to work with. Today, we're going to explore why the Stirling approximation works so well.
2. [20s] Factorial function, continuous curve. -- The factorial function, denoted by n!, gives the product of all positive integers up to n. For example, 5! is 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1, which equals 120. Now, if we plot these discrete points, we can see how the factorial function grows. But what if we want to find a smooth curve that approximates this function?
3. [20s] Stirling approximation formula. -- Enter the Stirling approximation. It's given by the formula n! is approximately equal to the square root of 2 pi n, times n to the power of n, times e to the power of negative n. This formula looks a bit complex, but it's actually quite powerful. It allows us to estimate factorials for large n using continuous curves.
4. [22s] Natural logarithm transformation. -- Now, you might be wondering why we need to take the natural logarithm of both sides. Well, it turns out that working with logarithms can simplify things. The natural logarithm of n factorial is approximately n times the natural logarithm of n, minus n, plus the natural logarithm of 2 pi n, all divided by 2. This is the logarithmic form of the Stirling approximation.
5. [19s] Integral approximation, continuous curve. -- The key to understanding why the Stirling approximation works lies in the integral approximation of the natural logarithm. The natural logarithm of n factorial can be approximated by the integral from 1 to n of the natural logarithm of x, dx. This integral gives us a smooth curve that approximates the discrete points of the factorial function.
6. [20s] Euler-Maclaurin formula. -- To get a more accurate approximation, we can use the Euler-Maclaurin formula. It's a formula that relates the sum of a function to an integral plus a series of correction terms. The first correction term is the average of the function evaluated at the endpoints. This term accounts for the fact that the factorial function is discrete, not continuous.

REQUEST
How does uniform continuity differ from ordinary continuity across an entire graph?

BEATS SO FAR
  (nothing yet — open the explanation)

Write the next 6 beat(s), numbered from 1. Stop early and write END if the explanation is complete.

1. [24s] Function graph with vertical strip. -- Imagine a function f(x) plotted on a graph. Now, let's take a vertical strip of fixed width, say 2ε, centered around a point x = a. This strip represents the wiggle room we're allowed when defining continuity. The height of the function at x = a is f(a), and within this strip, the function values must stay within ε of f(a). This is the definition of continuity at x = a.
2. [21s] Continuity at a point. -- Continuity at a point means that for every ε > 0, there exists a δ > 0 such that for all x within δ of a, the function values f(x) are within ε of f(a). In other words, as x gets closer to a, f(x) gets closer to f(a). This is the classic definition of continuity, and it's what we've all learned in calculus.
3. [22s] Sliding strip across graph. -- Now, let's slide this vertical strip along the graph. As we move the strip, the required δ might change to keep the function values within ε of f(a). For example, if the function has a steep slope near a, we might need a smaller δ to keep the function values within ε. This shows that δ can depend on both ε and the point a.
4. [25s] Uniform continuity definition. -- Uniform continuity is a stronger condition. It requires that the same δ works for all x in the domain. In other words, for every ε > 0, there exists a δ > 0 such that for all x and y in the domain, if |x - y| < δ, then |f(x) - f(y)| < ε. This means the wiggle room δ doesn't depend on the specific point a, but is global for the entire domain.
5. [23s] Uniform continuity example. -- Let's look at an example. Consider the function f(x) = x^2. For this function, the required δ depends on the point a. Near a = 0, a small δ works because the function is flat. But as we move away from 0, we need a larger δ to keep the function values within ε. This shows that f(x) = x^2 is not uniformly continuous on the real line.
6. [17s] Uniform continuity on closed interval. -- Now, let's restrict f(x) = x^2 to a closed interval, say [0, 1]. On this interval, the function is continuous and the slopes are bounded. This means that the required δ can be chosen independently of the point a within [0, 1]. Therefore, f(x) = x^2 is uniformly continuous on [0, 1].

1. [22s] Definition of continuity on a graph. -- Continuity is a fundamental concept in mathematics that describes the behavior of functions. A function is continuous if it has no jumps, breaks, or holes in its graph. This means that as the input approaches any point in the domain, the output approaches the value of the function at that point. But is this enough? Are there functions that are continuous but not uniform continuous?
2. [25s] Definition of uniform continuity on a graph. -- Uniform continuity is a stronger condition than regular continuity. A function is uniformly continuous if the change in the output is uniformly bounded by the change in the input, no matter where the input is in the domain. This means that for any two points in the domain, the difference in their outputs is less than or equal to a constant times the difference in their inputs. But why do we need this stronger condition?
3. [31s] Example of a continuous but not uniformly continuous function. -- Consider the function f(x) = 1/x on the interval (0,1). This function is continuous on the open interval (0,1), but it is not uniformly continuous. To see why, let's take two points x and y in the interval (0,1) such that y is very close to x. The difference in their outputs is |f(x) - f(y)| = |1/x - 1/y| = |(y - x)/(xy)|. As x approaches 0, the denominator xy approaches 0, and the difference in the outputs can become arbitrarily large, no matter how small the difference in the inputs is.
4. [45s] Graph of f(x) = 1/x and f(x) = 1/x^2. -- Now, consider the function f(x) = 1/x^2 on the interval (0,1). This function is uniformly continuous on the interval (0,1). To see why, let's take two points x and y in the interval (0,1) such that y is very close to x. The difference in their outputs is |f(x) - f(y)| = |1/x^2 - 1/y^2| = |(y^2 - x^2)/(x^2 y^2)| = |(y - x)(y + x)/(x^2 y^2)|. Since x and y are in the interval (0,1), the term (y + x) is less than or equal to 2, and the term (x^2 y^2) is greater than or equal to x^2 y^2. Therefore, the difference in the outputs is less than or equal to 2|y - x|/x^2 y^2. As x approaches 0, the denominator x^2 y^2 approaches 0, but the difference in the outputs is still bounded by a constant times the difference in the inputs.
5. [33s] Graph of f(x) = 1/x and f(x) = 1/x^2 with zoom-in. -- The key difference between these two functions is the rate at which they approach infinity as x approaches 0. The function f(x) = 1/x approaches infinity much faster than the function f(x) = 1/x^2. This means that for the function f(x) = 1/x, the difference in the outputs can become arbitrarily large for arbitrarily small differences in the inputs, no matter where the inputs are in the domain. However, for the function f(x) = 1/x^2, the difference in the outputs is uniformly bounded by the difference in the inputs, no matter where the inputs are in the domain.
6. [27s] Definition of Lipschitz continuity. -- Lipschitz continuity is a special case of uniform continuity. A function is Lipschitz continuous if the change in the output is bounded by a constant times the change in the input. This means that for any two points in the domain, the difference in their outputs is less than or equal to a constant times the difference in their inputs. The function f(x) = 1/x^2 is Lipschitz continuous on the interval (0,1), but the function f(x) = 1/x is not.

Huffman coding is a lossless data compression algorithm that uses variable-length codewords to represent source symbols. It was developed by David A. Huffman in 1952 and is widely used in various applications, from file compression to data transmission. The key idea behind Huffman coding is to assign shorter codewords to more frequent symbols and longer codewords to less frequent ones, thereby reducing the overall size of the data.
2. [24s] Bar chart of symbol frequencies. -- To understand how Huffman coding works, let's start by considering a simple example. Suppose we have a set of symbols with their respective frequencies. For instance, let's say we have symbols A, B, C, D, and E with frequencies 45%, 13%, 12%, 16%, and 14% respectively. Our goal is to assign binary codewords to these symbols in such a way that the most frequent symbols have the shortest codewords, and vice versa.
3. [26s] Animated process of building a Huffman tree. -- The first step in Huffman coding is to build a binary tree, known as the Huffman tree, which will help us assign the codewords. We start by creating a leaf node for each symbol and assign it a probability equal to the frequency of the symbol. Then, we repeatedly combine the two least probable nodes into a new node, with the sum of their probabilities, until only one node remains, which becomes the root of the tree.
4. [29s] Huffman tree with assigned codewords. -- Once we have the Huffman tree, we can assign binary codewords to each symbol by traversing the tree from the root to the leaf node corresponding to the symbol. For each left branch we take, we append a '0' to the codeword, and for each right branch, we append a '1'. For example, if we have a Huffman tree where the most frequent symbol A is at the leftmost leaf, its codeword would be '0', and the next most frequent symbol B would be '10', and so on.
5. [27s] Original and compressed data side by side. -- Now, let's see how Huffman coding works in practice. Suppose we have a string of symbols "AABACAADAABBAA" based on the frequencies we discussed earlier. Without any compression, this string would require 14 bits to represent each symbol, resulting in a total of 140 bits. However, using Huffman coding, we can represent the same string with fewer bits. For instance, if A is '0', B is '10', C is '110', D is '1110', and E is '1111', the compressed string would be '00100110001011101010010'.
6. [24s] Comparison of original and compressed data sizes. -- To see the benefits of Huffman coding, let's compare the sizes of the original and compressed data. The original string "AABACAADAABBAA" has 14 symbols, each represented by 8 bits (assuming ASCII encoding), resulting in a total of 112 bits. The compressed string, on the other hand, has a total of 30 bits, which is a significant reduction in size. This shows how Huffman coding can effectively compress data by using variable-length codewords.

1. [21s] Binary data transmission with noise. -- Imagine you're sending a message across a noisy communication channel. The message is represented as a sequence of binary digits, or bits, which can be either 0 or 1. However, due to the noise in the channel, some of these bits might get flipped, turning a 0 into a 1 or vice versa. This corruption can lead to errors in the received message.
2. [33s] Binary data with parity bit. -- One simple way to detect errors is to add a parity bit to the message. The parity bit is a single bit that is added to the end of the message to make the total number of 1s either even or odd, depending on the chosen parity. For example, if we choose even parity, the parity bit will be 0 if the number of 1s in the message is even, and 1 if it's odd. The receiver can then count the number of 1s in the received message, including the parity bit, to check if the parity is correct.
3. [27s] Binary data with parity bit and error detection. -- If the received message has the correct parity, the receiver can be confident that the message has been transmitted correctly. However, if the received message has an incorrect parity, the receiver knows that an error has occurred. But this method can only detect errors, not correct them. If a single bit is flipped, the parity will be incorrect, and the error will be detected. But if two bits are flipped, the parity will be correct, and the error will go undetected.
4. [26s] Binary data with Hamming code and error correction. -- To both detect and correct errors, we can use a more sophisticated error-correcting code, such as the Hamming code. The Hamming code adds multiple parity bits to the message, which are placed in specific positions within the message. These parity bits are calculated based on the values of the other bits in the message. The receiver can then use these parity bits to not only detect errors but also to identify the exact bit that has been corrupted.
5. [39s] Binary data with Hamming code and error correction example. -- For example, let's say we have a 4-bit message, and we want to use a Hamming code to protect it. We would first add three parity bits to the message, placing them in positions that are powers of 2, i.e., positions 1, 2, and 4. The values of these parity bits would be calculated based on the values of the other bits in the message. The receiver would then use these parity bits to check the consistency of the received message. If the parity bits are correct, the message is assumed to be error-free. If one of the parity bits is incorrect, the receiver can identify the exact bit that has been corrupted and correct it.
6. [25s] Binary data with Hamming code and error correction visualization. -- To visualize how the Hamming code works, we can represent the message and the parity bits as a grid, with the parity bits in the first row and the message bits in the subsequent rows. The parity bits are calculated by performing a bitwise XOR operation on the message bits in specific columns. The receiver can then use these parity bits to check the consistency of the received message and, if necessary, correct any errors.

1. [19s] Graph with labeled vertices and edges. -- Turán's theorem is a fundamental result in extremal graph theory, which deals with the maximum or minimum number of edges a graph can have under certain conditions. Today, we're going to explore this theorem and understand how it determines the maximum number of edges a graph can have without containing a specific complete subgraph, known as a clique.
2. [20s] Complete graph (clique) illustration. -- A clique is a subset of vertices in a graph where every two distinct vertices are connected by an edge. Turán's theorem provides a formula to calculate the maximum number of edges a graph can have without containing a clique of a given size. This is crucial in various applications, such as network design, coding theory, and even social network analysis.
3. [27s] Graph partitioned into smaller complete graphs. -- The theorem is named after Pál Turán, who first published it in 1941. Turán's theorem states that for a given number of vertices n and a given clique size r, the maximum number of edges a graph can have without containing a clique of size r is achieved by a complete r-partite graph where the vertices are divided into r equal or nearly equal parts, and every vertex in one part is connected to every vertex in the other parts.
4. [18s] Equation for Turán's theorem. -- The formula for the maximum number of edges, denoted as ex(n, r), is given by ex(n, r) = (1 - 1/r) * n² / 2. This formula is derived by considering the complete r-partite graph that Turán's theorem guarantees will have the maximum number of edges without containing a clique of size r.
5. [22s] Example with n=7 and r=3. -- Let's consider an example to understand this better. Suppose we have a graph with 7 vertices and we want to find the maximum number of edges it can have without containing a clique of size 3. According to Turán's theorem, we should partition the 7 vertices into 3 equal or nearly equal parts. So, we'll have two parts with 2 vertices and one part with 3 vertices.
6. [22s] Complete tripartite graph illustration. -- The complete tripartite graph K_{2,2,3} will have the maximum number of edges without containing a clique of size 3. Each vertex in the first part is connected to every vertex in the second and third parts, and similarly for the other parts. The total number of edges in this graph is calculated using the formula ex(7, 3) = (1 - 1/3) * 7² / 2 = 14.
